artworks.title: On the Yacht “Namouna,” Venice
artworks.current_collection: Wadsworth Atheneum Museum of Art, Hartford
artworks.image_alt: Guests relaxing on the shaded deck of a yacht: a woman in a white skirt leans on the cabin, men in summer suits sit and read, and a dog rests at their feet, with the sea beyond.
artworks.observation: Boat is rocking, gazes are also rocking.
artworks.excerpt: Behind the serenity of a yacht deck in Venice, Stewart’s painting balances tranquility with tension, revealing an intricate web of interpersonal relationships.
artworks.first_encounter: I first met this painting on our class’s first visit to the Wadsworth, for CL English Seminar: Writing About Art. The canvas is huge, and there was so much happening inside it that I was intrigued at once. Everything seemed to move: I could almost feel the deck rocking beneath me, and imagined myself growing a little seasick.
artworks.behind_canvas:
Julius LeBlanc Stewart (1855–1919) was an American painter born in Philadelphia who spent most of his working life in Paris, where he became known for large, polished scenes of fashionable society.1

The Namouna was the steam yacht of James Gordon Bennett Jr., the publisher of the New York Herald. Stewart painted a party of guests aboard her in Venice in 1890.1
artworks.looking_closer:
All Eyes on Deck!

The scene

On The Yacht “Namouna” Venice is an oil painting on a 56-by-77-inch canvas completed in 1890 by Julius LeBlanc Stewart, now displayed in the Wadsworth Atheneum Museum of Art in Hartford, Connecticut. Stewart depicts five passengers and a sailor aboard a private yacht, its polished wooden deck sheltered beneath an expansive white canopy. The passengers occupy distinct positions: a woman stands beside the wooden cabin on the left, a man sits farther back, a woman in coral occupies the center, and a woman and a man sit close together on the right. A dog rests with the seated pair, while the sailor stands near the vessel’s distant end. At first glance, the painting presents an idyllic scene of leisure.

Line and movement

Upon initial viewing, Stewart constructs an opulent retreat through the painting’s expansive composition, fluid lines, and carefully modulated light. The horizontally elongated painting stretches the yacht’s deck laterally across the viewer’s field of vision, allowing the passengers to occupy the foreground without appearing crowded. This lateral openness is enhanced by diagonal lines. The deck’s planks, metal railings, and canopy framework recede toward a vanishing region in the upper right. Their convergence establishes depth while drawing the viewer’s eye along the vessel and eventually to its endpoint. The slanted perspective mimics fluid forward movement, preventing the broad horizontal canvas from becoming static.

Stewart extends this sense of movement through clothing. A gentle, pleasant breeze is indicated through the leftmost woman’s long skirt gathering in soft, irregular folds rendered in smoothly blended brushstrokes, its curved contours contrasting with the straight lines of the deck. Likewise, the sailor’s navy ribbon billows away from his body, loose and fluttering, reinforcing the agreeable weather. Through the use of both rigid structural lines and flowing organic forms, Stewart grants the scene a subtle sense of motion.

Light under the canopy

Similarly, the enormous triangular canopy above the passengers transforms the role of sunlight into one of comfort. The sunlight’s intensity is evident in the sharp highlights scattered across the ocean, metal railings, glass, and the canopy’s edges, where brilliant white illumination meets deep shadows, producing pronounced tonal contrasts. Yet before this harsh light reaches the deck, the broad, pale canopy, occupying much of the upper composition, filters it into a soft glow, rendered through muted colors and warm highlights. These passengers thus enjoy the pleasures of the outdoors while remaining physically sheltered from its harsher elements, signaling a comfortable, protected retreat.

A moment of repose

Within this sheltered space, the two figures in navy on the right are particularly prominent. Painted in a darker shade, the pair holds the strongest concentration of low values amid whites, creams, and pale shades, as if pocketed in the shadows. The reclining woman’s curved posture, loosely extended leg and foot, and tilted head resting on a pillow establish an impression of serenity. The dog is draped comfortably across her lap, its half-closed eyes exaggerating the sense of drowsiness and security. It repeats her diagonal orientation, creating a visual rhythm of relaxed, downward-sloping forms. The relatively upright man reading beside her creates a contrasting vertical axis, heightening the sense of ease. By surrounding these stationary bodies with calm movements, like the traveling yacht, mollified sunlight, and soothing breeze, Stewart invites the audience into a moment of repose.
artworks.what_i_see:
Human desire and interpersonal relationships.

A stage

Yet the composition that creates this tranquility simultaneously introduces underlying tension. Although the horizontal format and receding perspectives suggest openness, the painting is cropped tightly around the five figures, causing the deck to resemble a theatrical stage. The viewer sees neither the yacht in its entirety nor much of the surrounding world, as even the ocean and sky are confined to a narrow opening between the canopy and boat. The tight enclosure concentrates attention on the individuals and their interactions. Their arrangement further makes the seemingly candid snapshot feel choreographed: they form a loose triangle across the deck, with both the outer figures’ heads turned inward, preventing the viewer’s focus from escaping this group. Repeated triangular configurations appear via the canopy’s angular edges above and the yacht’s narrowing perspective, echoed by the smaller clusters of bodies and negative spaces, eliminating any sense of arbitrariness.

The pair in navy

Within this stage-like composition, Stewart’s carefully choreographed figures transform the deck into a stage for human interaction. Even the navy pair, previously distinguished by the woman’s relaxed posture and visual cohesion, has an underlying layer of intimacy. Their similarly dark clothing overlaps into a nearly continuous mass, merging their silhouettes. Their legs extend along parallel diagonals, while their upper bodies incline toward the shared book, their gazes converging upon it in a triangular form. The small negative space, unlike the broad intervals separating the other passengers, underscores their proximity, creating an impression of intimacy.

The woman in coral

From this satisfied pair, Stewart draws the eye leftward to the woman seated in the center, along a shared diagonal. Her vivid orange-pink clothing separates her chromatically from the navy pair, yet her torso turns toward the man, as her gaze extends across the space, directly to him, connecting her to the pair. Stewart also illuminates her face and upper body with relatively bright highlights, emphasizing her transfixed gaze on the man’s face, which is in stark contrast with the pair’s line of sight, both directed to the book. Her slightly parted lips become pronounced as well, making the movement stand out even more since none of the other passengers’ mouths are open. Her hand grips the chair behind her, introducing a taut tension absent from the woman in navy and her softened contours.

The disparity between the two is even more notable due to the broad, inverted triangular negative space between them, created as they are leaning in the opposite direction. Juxtaposed with the narrow, enclosed negative space between the navy pair, the wide, open gap accentuates the central woman’s lack of physical proximity with the man despite her apparent fascination with him.

The pair in white

On the left, Stewart constructs another relationship through lighter hues and directional movement. The leftmost man and woman face each other, forming a loosely enclosed triangle that echoes the arrangement of the navy pair. Both figures wear white, creating a chromatic connection like the navy pair, although their silhouettes remain more distinct than them. Another distinguishing factor is the color of the woman’s blouse. The pale pink echoes the clothing of the central figure, establishing another chromatic relationship across the otherwise separated groups.

Yet unlike the central woman’s gaze, which travels across a large interval and is unmet by another, the leftmost woman’s gaze is met by the man within her immediate space, suggesting a mutual engagement resembling the fulfilled intimacy of the navy pair. Her upper body curves in the direction of the man, and the man is in the process of standing or shifting forward towards her, disrupting the otherwise rigid vertical posture. The converging postures emphasize mutual inclination towards each other. The woman, however, is differentiated from the rightmost woman once again through her action of gripping the railing, which simultaneously supports and restrains her, creating a subtle tension of craving and inhibition.

The sailor

Even the distant sailor, detached from the group of passengers, contributes to this chain of social dynamics. Positioned near the receding end of the yacht, he appears considerably smaller than the foreground passengers, and his figure is partially absorbed into the complex arrangement of railings and equipment—clearly a part of the background. His upright posture echoes the vertical structures surrounding him, while his less distinctly rendered features reduce his visual prominence. Unlike the group, whose bodies and gazes are oriented toward one another, he faces outward, aimed at the space beyond the yacht. Stewart uses this opposing direction of attention as a foil to the group’s inward engagement, emphasizing the passengers’ enclosed network of interactions.

Tranquility and tension

Ultimately, behind the apparent serenity painted by the expansive format, polished surfaces, softened illumination, and reclining bodies, the tight framing, uneven spatial distances, wandering eyes, and contrasting postures create constant psychological movement. Through these formal contrasts, Stewart’s painting balances tranquility with tension, revealing an intricate web of interpersonal relationships beneath the yacht’s seemingly effortless leisure.

marginalia.body: I’m wondering more about the woman on the left. We cannot see her face, and, unlike the other two women, she is not framed by the men.
Is there a connection between her and the distant sailor worth considering?

sources.text: Wadsworth Atheneum Museum of Art, Hartford. Collection record for Julius LeBlanc Stewart, On the Yacht “Namouna,” Venice, 1890.

artworks.current_collection: Wadsworth Atheneum Museum of Art, Hartford
artworks.excerpt: This painting, caught in between destruction and revolution, was an invitation to imagine.
artworks.first_encounter:
I was captivated by this during our first visit to Wadsworth, but ditched it for a more… “dynamic” painting, because I instinctively knew I was going to have thoughts wandering off this painting. But this was, without doubt, the painting that was able to hold me in a trance. Growing up as an only child, building worlds were a daily hobby—whether through books, movies, series, or art, I was constantly living out my imagination. This painting, caught in between destruction and revolution, was an invitation to imagine.

I had so many questions: What caused those pillars to fall? What grandness stood before? Who is ruling this ruin now? That thick pillar looks great to hop on top of and perhaps, a leader of a revolution, to speak in a charismatic, booming voice. What is the tiny city just beyond? Are they related to this destroyed structure? Does the volcano have a story?

Just the sheer volume of questions and stories that rush to me is what keeps me glued here.
artworks.behind_canvas:
Thomas Cole (1801–1848) was born in Lancashire, England, and emigrated with his family to the United States in 1818. He is regarded as the founder of the Hudson River School, the first American movement of landscape painting.2

Cole travelled in Europe several times. On his last trip, in 1842, he visited Sicily and sketched Mount Etna from Taormina, on the island’s eastern coast. Back in his studio he worked those sketches up into paintings like this one, dated 1843.2

The ruins in the foreground are the ancient theatre of Taormina, built by the Greeks and later rebuilt by the Romans. Beyond them rises Etna, the highest active volcano in Europe, with the coastline of the Ionian Sea curving away to the left.1

Ruined civilizations were a lifelong subject for Cole. His five-painting series The Course of Empire (1833–36) follows a single imagined landscape from wilderness through a great empire to its destruction and abandoned ruins.3
artworks.behind_interpretation: Writers on Cole often read his Italian ruins alongside The Course of Empire: crumbling stone that speaks of how short-lived human power is, set against a mountain that was there long before it and will outlast it.2 The smoke rising from Etna’s summit can be read the same way: the land itself is still alive and still changing, while the empire that built the theatre is gone.
artworks.what_i_see: I saw this as both destruction and revolution: a land that remembers history, wrongfully taken away, and maybe, this time, rightfully fixed. After all, history is a story. Humans are volatile and unreliable. But land is a different story. Land remembers.
artworks.conversations: Makes me think of Fourth Wing. Stones don’t burn in Aretia, but what if it was destroyed?

marginalia.body: Why am I so attracted to this painting?
It has become my computer wallpaper and I am simply in love with it.

sources.text: Wadsworth Atheneum Museum of Art, Hartford. Collection record for Thomas Cole, Mount Etna from Taormina, 1843.
Ellwood C. Parry III, The Art of Thomas Cole: Ambition and Imagination. Newark: University of Delaware Press, 1988.
New-York Historical Society. Thomas Cole, The Course of Empire (five paintings), 1833–36.

artworks.title: Mount Etna from Taormina
artworks.image_alt: The ruins of an ancient theatre in the foreground, with a smoking, snow-capped Mount Etna rising over a wide valley and coastline at dawn.

artworks.excerpt: Harsh, vivid strokes ripple across a golden field under Mont Sainte-Victoire. It feels like fall.
artworks.first_encounter: The harsh and vivid lines create ripples across the golden, lush field. Even the sky feels like it’s rippling. It feels like fall.
artworks.behind_canvas:
Pierre-Auguste Renoir (1841–1919) was one of the founding painters of French Impressionism, alongside Claude Monet, with whom he painted side by side in the late 1860s.2

Mont Sainte-Victoire rises east of Aix-en-Provence in southern France. It is best known through Paul Cézanne, who painted it dozens of times. In the late 1880s Renoir stayed near Aix and worked alongside Cézanne, and he painted the mountain during those visits.2

By then Renoir had grown dissatisfied with Impressionism’s soft, dissolving touch. In the mid-1880s he turned to firmer drawing and sharper, drier color, a phase sometimes called his manière aigre, or “sour manner.”2
artworks.behind_interpretation: The parallel, slanting strokes are often linked to Cézanne’s influence: Cézanne built his pictures from blocks of directional strokes, and here Renoir seems to borrow that structure while keeping his own heat of color. It may be part of why the painting looks like Monet at first glance and then feels much harsher.
artworks.looking_closer:
At first it seemed similar to Monet, but I realized the line strokes and colors were much harsher.

Nothing here is blended. The sky is built from long diagonal strokes that all slant the same way, down and to the right, so the blue reads less like air and more like something falling or blowing through the picture. The field below is laid in with shorter, flatter strokes of yellow and ochre, dragged sideways, which is why it seems to move in waves rather than lie still.

The trees are made differently again: small, curved dabs stacked into rounded masses. The olive trees in the middle are a cool blue-green, set between hot orange and red on one side and a deep, heavy green on the other. Renoir puts warm and cool colors right next to each other instead of mixing them, and that friction is what makes the colors feel loud.

The mountain itself is pale lavender and rose, the softest thing in the painting. It sits far back, quiet, while everything in front of it vibrates.

marginalia.body: The trees are like in progression??? From summer to fall.

sources.text: Yale University Art Gallery, New Haven. Collection record for Pierre-Auguste Renoir, La Montagne Sainte-Victoire.
John House and Anne Distel, Renoir. London: Arts Council of Great Britain, 1985.

artworks.title: La Montagne Sainte-Victoire
artworks.image_alt: Mont Sainte-Victoire in violet and pink beyond rows of blue-green trees and a field of golden grass, in quick, feathery brushstrokes.

artworks.excerpt: Hope and sadness coexist. Is it sunrise or sunset?
artworks.first_encounter: Hope and sadness coexist. Is it sunrise or sunset? To me, it feels like sunrise, and the boat is heading out into the bigger world.
artworks.behind_canvas:
Fitz Henry Lane (1804–1865) was born in Gloucester, Massachusetts. A childhood illness left him unable to walk without crutches. He trained as a lithographer in Boston before turning to marine painting.2

For more than a century he was known as “Fitz Hugh Lane,” a mistake that was corrected through research by the Cape Ann Museum in Gloucester in the 2000s.3

In the 1850s Lane made repeated trips along the coast of Maine, sketching harbors such as Camden on Penobscot Bay, and painted this scene in 1851.1 His calm, precisely lit harbor views were later grouped by twentieth-century historians under the name “Luminism.”2
artworks.looking_closer:
The light comes from one low point near the center of the horizon, behind the hills. Right at the waterline the sky is a hot peach that cools upward into pale green and then a deep blue-gray at the top of the canvas. The clouds are lit from below, pink only on their undersides, which means the sun is still under the horizon, not above it.

The water is almost completely still. It holds a soft copy of the sky and the ship, with only a few faint ripples where the small rowboat on the left breaks the surface. There are no visible brushstrokes anywhere; the paint is smoothed until the surface feels like glass.

Everything solid is dark. The ship, the rocks and the headland are near-silhouettes against the glow, and the lighthouse is the only pale, upright form on the right. The ship’s sails hang half-loose, not yet full of wind, so it sits in the moment just before moving.

The sky takes up more than half the painting, and the ship and the lighthouse face each other across an open stretch of water in the middle. That gap is where the light is brightest.
artworks.conversations: Reminds me of Spider-Man: Brand New Day, because it’s like a new day, a new beginning, despite all the sorrows of the past.

marginalia.body: Do some people see this as sunset? Am I seeing it as sunrise because of my psychological state?

sources.text: Yale University Art Gallery, New Haven. Collection record for Fitz Henry Lane, Lighthouse at Camden, Maine, 1851.
John Wilmerding, Fitz Hugh Lane. New York: Praeger, 1971.
Cape Ann Museum, Gloucester, Massachusetts. Research on the name of Fitz Henry Lane.

artworks.title: Lighthouse at Camden, Maine
artworks.image_alt: A sailing ship at rest on still water at dusk, a man rowing a small boat beside it, and a white lighthouse on a dark rocky point under a glowing sky.

artworks.excerpt: It’s HUGE. And yet so intricate. It feels like there are human bodies wrapped inside.
artworks.first_encounter: Ok, it’s HUGE. And yet so intricate. It feels like there are human bodies wrapped inside.
artworks.behind_canvas:
El Anatsui (born 1944) is a Ghanaian sculptor who has lived and worked in Nsukka, Nigeria, for most of his career, teaching for decades at the University of Nigeria.2

Since the late 1990s he has been best known for monumental wall hangings like this one, made from thousands of flattened aluminum bottle caps and liquor-bottle wrappers, joined together with copper wire. Because the metal “cloth” is flexible, it is folded and shaped differently each time it is hung.2

In 2015 he received the Golden Lion for Lifetime Achievement at the Venice Biennale.2
artworks.behind_interpretation: The hangings are often read through cloth: Anatsui has connected them to kente and other West African textiles, and to the history of liquor as a trade good between Europe, Africa and the Americas. The bottle caps carry that history inside something that looks, from across the room, like a precious gold fabric.2
artworks.looking_closer:
Up close the surface breaks apart into thousands of small units: gold discs packed tightly together across the middle, and around the edges, rows of narrow rectangular strips in red, yellow, black and cream, lined up like stitches or woven bands. The border reads almost like a frame, or like the edge of a textile, while the gold field inside it swells and spills over.

It isn’t flat. The whole thing has been gathered, pushed and folded so that it bulges out from the wall in ridges and hollows. Light catches on the high points and drops into shadow in the folds, so the gold is never one color: it shifts from bright yellow to bronze to almost brown depending on where it bends.

The bottom edge doesn’t end in a straight line. It frays into loose, uneven tabs, the way fabric does when it isn’t hemmed. Standing in front of it with someone beside you, the scale becomes physical: the people are smaller than a single fold.

sources.text: Yale University Art Gallery, New Haven. Collection record for El Anatsui, Society Woman’s Cloth (Gold).
Susan Mullin Vogel, El Anatsui: Art and Life. Munich: Prestel, 2012.

artworks.title: Society Woman’s Cloth (Gold)
artworks.image_alt: Two visitors stand before a vast, rippling wall hanging of gold, red and black metal pieces in a gallery.

artworks.current_collection: Wadsworth Atheneum Museum of Art, Hartford
artworks.excerpt: A sunlit coast on Mount Desert Island, and a huge sense of loss and sorrow beneath the brightness.
artworks.first_encounter: I thought the water droplets would splash onto me, and I could hear the harsh yet calming sound of wave crashing on the rocks. Even though the sun is up in the sky and the painting is pretty bright, I felt a huge sense of loss and sorrow in this.
artworks.behind_canvas:
Frederic Edwin Church (1826–1900) was born in Hartford, Connecticut. In 1844 he became the pupil of Thomas Cole, the founder of the Hudson River School, and went on to be one of the best-known American painters of his day, famous for vast, minutely detailed landscapes.2

Church first travelled to Mount Desert Island, on the coast of Maine, in 1850 and returned several times, drawn by its granite cliffs and heavy surf. He painted this view of the island’s shore in 1863.1
artworks.behind_interpretation: The painting was made in the middle of the American Civil War. Writers on Church have read the stormy skies and turbulent seas of his work from these years against the national crisis; whether or not he meant it, the bright sun over a violent, breaking sea holds both calm and upheaval at once.2
artworks.what_i_see:
can the ocean cry?
its tears glitter in sorrow, churning,
mourning what has sunk deep
sunk & drunk & chewed thoroughly
its tears shine and splatter, spitting
up what it could not digest
its hands reach and grab and yet
even the smallest are simply slipping, too
easy to escape
& drowning, smothered by its palms
it’s wailing at its destruction, gurgling
in fear—or perhaps woe, who knows—of what
it sees
can the ocean cry?

sources.text: Wadsworth Atheneum Museum of Art, Hartford. Collection record for Frederic Edwin Church, Coast Scene, Mount Desert, 1863.
Franklin Kelly, Frederic Edwin Church and the National Landscape. Washington, D.C.: Smithsonian Institution Press, 1988.

artworks.title: Coast Scene, Mount Desert
artworks.image_alt: Waves crash white against dark rocks on a rugged coast, under a hazy sun burning through pink and violet clouds.

artworks.excerpt: Like a kaleidoscope: the excitement of a younger me running around amusement parks.
artworks.first_encounter: I’m swirling with the thousands of things going on; it’s like a kaleidoscope. I feel the excitement of younger me running around amusement parks, when the scariest thing ever was the House of Horror and the Viking.
artworks.behind_canvas:
Joseph Stella (1877–1946) was born in Muro Lucano, in southern Italy, and emigrated to New York in 1896.2

Between 1909 and 1912 he lived in Europe, where he saw the work of the Italian Futurists, painters who broke their subjects into fragments of color and line to convey speed, noise and modern machinery.2

Back in New York he painted Battle of Lights, Coney Island, Mardi Gras (1913–14), the electric spectacle of the amusement park during its Mardi Gras festival. It became one of the first major Futurist paintings made in America.1
artworks.behind_interpretation: Stella doesn’t paint what Coney Island looked like so much as what it felt like to be inside it: the crush of bodies, the noise, the rides and thousands of electric bulbs all at once. The fragmentation is the experience.
artworks.looking_closer:
I see the details of the amusement park?

Nothing is whole. The canvas is shattered into hundreds of small, hard-edged pieces, triangles, crescents, zigzags, wedges, so that you never see a ride or a person, only the feeling of them going past too fast. Long beams of white cut diagonally across from the upper left like searchlights, and everything else seems to spin outward from a tall, glowing tower in the center.

The colors are almost all at full strength: emerald, cobalt, scarlet, orange, white, laid side by side with very little shadow between them. Where a shadow should be, there is just another color. Even the darkest areas at the bottom are a deep red and green rather than black.

Look long enough and fragments of things surface and then disappear again: strings of tiny lights, curling shapes like ribbons or roller-coaster track, and pieces of painted letters, as if from signs glimpsed in the crowd.
artworks.what_i_see:
I can still hear her.

“That one!” The bright voice is filled with such determination. Turning her back from the saccharine clouds of pink and sky-blue cotton candy, her eyes are glued to the glaring red sign that has five chilli peppers drawn on it, a clear warning to back off. She’s eyed it for a while, and pulls her dad’s meaty hands as she sprints for the flashy food truck.

Wiggling impatiently, she does a little happy dance as her dad pays, and doesn’t forget to chirp earnestly on tiptoes, “Extra hot sauce, please!”

The cashier raises his eyebrows, bending over to see the girl clearly, and points to the drawing.

She merely scoffs at the sign, though, and opens her jaw wide, biting into the hot sausage with extra hot sauce that her dad now holds. Her tiny fangs are accentuated by her missing front teeth, and she resembles a baby lion who thinks she is the biggest in her den. His nose crinkles as his lips waver in response to his daughter’s surprisingly gigantic bite, chuckling as he skillfully cups her chin, wiping off the sauce dribbling off her pink lips before it can stain her shirt.

“Good bite,” he says, smacking his own lips satisfactorily. Apple doesn’t fall far from the tree, does it? Like father, like daughter, the mother thinks, handing her husband another paper napkin. She’s shaking her head in feigned exasperation, but her folded, smiling eyes tell the truth, taking a smaller, slightly more civilized bite as her husband lifts the huge sausage to her mouth. After all that, he takes a bite himself. It is ingrained in his instinct to hand anything good to his daughter and wife, his favorite spicy snack not being an exception.

He barely has any time to gobble down the last bit before jogging after his daughter, who has pranced off into the playground, already playing captain, leading the other giggly kids around the pirate ship structure.

It’s been a sweetly exhausting day, …

To be continued.

sources.text: Yale University Art Gallery, New Haven. Collection record for Joseph Stella, Battle of Lights, Coney Island, Mardi Gras, 1913–14.
Irma B. Jaffe, Joseph Stella. Cambridge, Mass.: Harvard University Press, 1970.

artworks.title: Battle of Lights, Coney Island, Mardi Gras
artworks.image_alt: An explosion of fractured color: shards, arcs and starbursts of red, green, blue and white swirl around a glowing central tower.

artworks.excerpt: Time has stopped. Time, sound, everything.
artworks.first_encounter: Time has stopped. It feels like everything is just… stuck. Time, sound, everything.
artworks.behind_canvas:
Walter Tandy Murch (1907–1967) was born in Toronto and moved to New York as a young man, where he studied with the painter Arshile Gorky.1

He became known for quiet still lifes of ordinary mechanical objects, clocks, light bulbs, machine parts, painted in a soft, hazy light that makes them look both precise and slightly unreal.1
artworks.looking_closer:
The metronome is floating. It’s so dark.

It doesn’t quite sit on the ledge. There is a thin band of shadow under its base, as if it has lifted a few millimeters into the air. The pendulum is frozen off to one side instead of resting upright, caught in the middle of a beat that never finishes.

Almost all of the light in the painting is on the metronome itself: a warm glow on its front face and a bright orange strip in the slot behind the pendulum, like a light left on inside. Around it, the background isn’t flat black but a soft, mottled brown that seems to breathe, so the darkness has depth, like you could reach into it.

The small things are what make it strange: a pale rock perched on the metronome’s body with a thin string hanging down from it, and two more rocks on the ledge below. They don’t belong with a metronome, and the painting never explains them.
artworks.what_i_see: It feels so stuck and stifling, but it’s so magical and weird, like I’ll get absorbed into that darkness and get sucked up into it as well.

marginalia.body: What are those rocks? What’s that string protruding from the rock on top of the metronome?

sources.text: Archives of American Art, Smithsonian Institution. Walter Tandy Murch papers.

artworks.title: Metronome
artworks.image_alt: A wooden metronome, its pendulum stopped at an angle, seems to hover above a dark ledge with small rocks, against deep brown-black darkness.

artworks.excerpt: Finally, a real Basquiat. Human anatomy, turned into art.
artworks.first_encounter: What is this? Finally, a real Basquiat after getting (ragebaited????) by the Wadsworth, which had a similar style.
artworks.behind_canvas:
Jean-Michel Basquiat (1960–1988) was born in Brooklyn, New York, to a Haitian father and a Puerto Rican mother. In the late 1970s he first became known for the cryptic graffiti he wrote around Lower Manhattan under the tag SAMO, before becoming one of the most celebrated painters of the 1980s. He died in 1988, at 27.2

When he was seven he was hit by a car and spent weeks in the hospital. His mother gave him a copy of Gray’s Anatomy, the classic medical textbook, and its diagrams of bones, organs and muscles became a lasting source for his art.2

Words run through nearly all of his paintings. He often crossed words out, and said that doing so made people want to read them more.2
artworks.behind_interpretation: The anatomical labels can be read as a way of taking the body apart and naming it piece by piece, a cold, clinical language set against raw, hand-drawn marks. The result is half science diagram, half wall scrawl, which may be exactly why it feels both biological and ancient at once.
artworks.looking_closer:
Human anatomy, reminds me of biology. It’s really interesting how he depicted the body parts.

It is two panels hung side by side that behave like opposites. The left one is cream, crowded with small handwriting, numbers and rows of outlined feet or shoe soles, like a page torn from a notebook or a medical chart. The right one is mostly black, like a blackboard, and the marks on it are bigger, louder and hungrier: a head full of teeth, the word JAW, and a teal block where a dog-like face shouts WOOFS!

Words act as labels, the way they would in a textbook diagram, except they don’t always land where they should. LARINYX, a misspelled larynx, is written across a black, crowned head. THE ANKLE appears twice inside a red box, as if repeating it might make it true. Some words are crossed out but still perfectly readable.

The lines are fast and unpolished, drawn in oil stick and paint with no attempt to hide corrections. Red, blue and white arrows point in different directions, so your eye keeps jumping from label to label without ever finding the whole body.
artworks.conversations: Reminds me of Egyptian??? Or like cave art.
